prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Luggage, Nimbly, Eyes

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your poem, refined for greater lyrical flow and precision while preserving every image and idea from the original:

---

Luggage first, his suit jacket's lining trailing loose—
As always, just when hope had nearly failed you,
He slips nimbly from the taxi,
Eyes darting nervous, like brave crabs
Scuttling everywhere at once, guarding his papers.
He steers himself into the home berth,
Like a small tug amid a cloud of seagulls.
Worries flutter about him, thick and restless—
It takes him time to truly arrive.

And you wonder if he has ever known happiness:
When his blue eyes cloud
And drift toward the sea,
Is it only a daydream,
Or some long ache that renders him silent
In such gray, distant depths?
You will never know. But now,

Turning to you, his delicate mouth—
Like a magician's—
Turns curious, tender, full of quiet mischief,
Pursed like a wise old turtle's.
It seems he shares a secret
With the driver,
With the stewardess on the plane,
So that even as he opens his arms
And his warm voice folds around you,
Wrapping you in rough and tender bliss,
Just before you surrender to it entirely—

Suddenly, you remember:
The beloved does not arrive
From nowhere, self-made and alone.
Often he comes slowly, cautiously,
After a long ride through the city,
Past countless beautiful men and women,
And countless bodies laid to rest—
Mysterious, essential companions
Who traveled with him all along.

---

I preserved the poem's surreal, tender tone and its central meditation on arrival, hidden sorrow, and the quiet mysteries a beloved carries with him. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to rhythm, tone, or specific phrases.

outputs.L3:
# Arrival

He comes to us the way a small tug comes
through gulls and harbor noise—not gliding, but
nudging forward, anxious, cluttered, half
undone. He spills out of the taxi door
with luggage listing sideways, papers loose
and slipping from his arms like startled birds
he hasn't quite decided how to hold.
Nothing about his entrance says *arrival*
in the way we dreamed it—no clean parting
of the crowd, no music swelling up
to meet him. Just this fumbling, human weight
of a man trying to carry everything at once.

And I have wondered, watching him emerge
this way, if he has ever simply been
happy—not almost, not despite, not in
the pause between two griefs, but happy whole.
His eyes are blue the way a distance is
blue—blurred at the edges, holding something back,
some sorrow he has learned to fold so small
it fits inside a glance and disappears
before you're sure you saw it. Or perhaps
it's not sorrow at all, but a daydream
he visits when no one is watching, some
elsewhere he keeps returning to, alone.

Yet his mouth undoes all that. His mouth
is quick and sly, a magician's mouth, the kind
that promises a trick before he's shown
his hands. I've seen him charm the taxi driver
with some joke I didn't catch, seen him
lean toward a stewardess and watch her laugh
before she even knows she's laughing—as if
he carries small deceptions in his pockets,
harmless ones, just to prove the world
will still respond to him, still soften when
he asks it to. Strangers get this from him
freely, the parts of him that flicker light.

But when he finally turns to me, when arms
undo their tangle of luggage and reach instead
for me, his voice arrives before his hands—
low, warm, unhurried, saying my name
like it's a place he's glad to be returning to.
And I go under. Something in that voice
is bliss so full it borders on too much,
a warmth that pulls me sideways out of time
into a kind of trance where nothing else
insists on being noticed. Just this voice.
Just this arrival, finally complete.

Because he does not come to us instantly.
He does not simply appear, fully formed,
out of some clean and waiting nowhere. No—
he arrives the way all real things arrive:
slowly, deliberately, shaped by distance,
by the long unseen road that brought him here
past other cities, other rooms, other lives
he loved and lost and had to leave behind
to reach this door, this taxi, this cluttered
entrance into what we call *today*.
He is heavy with everywhere he's been.
That's why, when he holds you, it feels like homecoming—
not because he's new, but because he's traveled
so far, through so much, only to arrive.
outputs.L4:
**Arrival**

He comes by taxi, as he always does,
counting the fare before it's asked,
already reaching for his papers—
the ones he checks three times,
smoothing each corner like a wound
that might reopen if not tended.

I watch him from the window,
this small nervous man
navigating his own worry
like a small tug in a cloud of seagulls,
pushing forward through what circles him,
patient, insistent, entirely alone
in the noise he cannot hear.

What lives behind those blue eyes?
I have known him seasons now
and still cannot tell
if what I see is dreaming—
some quiet film played private
behind the pale iris—
or something older, tamped down,
a grief so long rehearsed
it has learned to look like calm.

He pays the driver with exact change,
counted twice. He does not look up
until he's certain of the door,
the number, the small brass plaque
that tells him he's arrived
at the place he meant to be.

*

I used to think love arrived
like weather, unannounced,
a gift dropped whole from some clear sky,
that the beloved simply *was*—
sudden, entire, without a history
that mattered more than this:
the fact of their arriving.

But watching him climb out,
papers gripped too tight,
counting his own change,
I understand something differently now.

No one arrives without their weather.
Every beloved is the last stop
on a long, uncertain route—
shaped by other rooms, other departures,
other hands that once let go
or never learned to hold on right.

He is not new. He is accumulated.
Every silence he carries
was built by someone before me,
every worried gesture
inherited from a life
I will never fully read,
blue eyes keeping their own weather,
their own private seagulls circling.

I did not choose him
out of nowhere.
I received him
the way you receive a coast—
shaped slowly by decades of water,
arriving as an accumulation of everything
that came before this quiet knock,
this taxi pulling away,
this man now walking toward me
with his whole uncertain history
folded like paper in his hands.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of What We Carry

Maria moved through the crowded terminal with unexpected grace, her worn suitcase trailing behind her like an obedient shadow. Most travelers seemed burdened by their belongings, shoulders hunched, faces tight with the stress of connections and schedules. But she navigated the chaos nimbly, weaving between families and business travelers with the practiced ease of someone who had learned that fighting the current only made the swim harder.

Her eyes told a different story than her movements suggested, though. While her body flowed effortlessly through the terminal—stepping around a spilled coffee, angling sideways through a bottleneck near security—her gaze held something heavier. There was a distance in them, a quality of looking through things rather than at them, as if she were seeing not the airport around her but somewhere else entirely.

An elderly man watched her pass, struck by the contradiction. Here was someone whose physical grace suggested lightness, whose luggage seemed to weigh nothing at all in her capable hands, yet whose eyes carried what looked like the accumulated weight of difficult decisions. He wondered, as strangers sometimes do in the anonymous intimacy of travel, what story lived behind that particular kind of tiredness.

We are all, perhaps, carrying two kinds of luggage—the visible kind that airlines can weigh and measure, and the invisible kind that shows up only in unguarded moments, in the set of someone's jaw or the way their eyes seem to focus on some middle distance that isn't quite there. Maria disappeared into her gate's boarding line, still moving nimbly, still carrying everything she owned in that one modest case, and something else entirely in the depths of her eyes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about someone anxiously waiting for a loved one to arrive from a trip, focusing on small physical details.
counterfactuals.output:
The Waiting

The kettle has gone cold twice now,
a skin forming on the tea
I keep forgetting to drink.

My thumbnail finds the seam
in the couch cushion, presses,
releases, presses again—
a small pulse I've made
without meaning to.

Outside, the streetlight flickers on
though it isn't dark yet,
just that gray hour
when headlights start to matter,
when every pair of them
becomes a question.

I've refolded the same towel
three times in the kitchen,
matching corners that don't need matching,
because my hands need something
to be right
when nothing else
can be confirmed.

The phone screen dims, lights up,
dims again from my checking—
no new messages,
just the last one, hours old:
*landed, love you, see you soon*
which was true then
and might still be true now
but the not-knowing
sits like a stone
under my sternum.

I notice the dog has stopped
pacing to the door with me,
has given up before I have,
curled into a comma
on the rug
while I keep standing,
keep listening
for the specific sound
of *that* car,
*that* engine,
the particular rhythm
of tires finding
the gravel by the mailbox.

My reflection in the dark window
looks older than I feel,
wire-tight shoulders,
a face arranged around
the shape of waiting.

Then—
headlights swing wide
into the driveway,
gravel under new sound,
and my whole body
remembers itself,
moves before I decide to move,
already reaching
for the door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem describing a father coming home, using imagery of taxis, luggage, and seagulls to evoke tension and love.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Return

A taxi door clicks shut like punctuation—
a sentence he's been forming for six months
now finally arriving at the curb.
The engine idles its small applause of exhaust
into evening air already thick with salt.

His suitcase drags one wheel, complains
against the pavement in a language
only distance teaches. I watch him lift it
anyway, the way you lift something
that has grown heavier than you remember,
though it holds the same three shirts,
the same worn paperback, unread.

Above us, gulls wheel and shriek—
those hinges of the sky swinging open, shut,
open again—hungry for whatever
the tide has left exposed. Their cries
sound almost like a question,
almost like the one I'm not asking:
*Did you miss this? Did you miss us?*

He stands there for a moment, keys
still in his pocket, looking at the house
like a man checking a photograph
against the real thing, matching up
the light in windows, the crooked mailbox,
the small ways nothing and everything changed.

I want to run. I want to stay planted
here on the porch step, arms crossed
like a customs agent, like someone
who has learned the cost of easy welcomes.

But then his suitcase hits the ground,
forgotten, and his arms open
the way the taxi door once did,
the way the gulls keep opening the sky,
and I am running down the steps
before I've decided to,
into the specific weather of his coat,
the smell of airports and elsewhere
and the particular way he says my name
like it's the only word
he's carried home that matters.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, image-rich poem about the arrival of "the beloved," blending airport imagery with metaphysical musings on happiness and secrecy.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Arrival

The beloved is coming through customs
with nothing to declare but light—
that old smuggler's trick, hiding
the sun inside a suitcase
lined with sleep.

Announcements fall from the ceiling
like broken angels learning language,
*Flight 000 now arriving from Nowhere,
please proceed to the gate marked Yes.*

I have been standing here since before
I was born, holding a sign
with my own name misspelled,
because the beloved always arrives
as someone you almost recognize—

the taste of a country you've never visited
but somehow remember the weather of.

Happiness works like this:
it clears security without a body,
walks past the metal detectors
of your ordinary Tuesday,
sets off nothing,
and yet the air changes composition,
becomes suddenly breathable
in a new direction.

The secret is that there is no secret—
just the beloved's coat, still smelling
of somewhere else,
draped over the back of a chair
in the food court where eternity
serves lukewarm coffee
and everyone is already home
but doesn't know it yet.

Outside, the planes keep landing,
bellies full of strangers
who are all, in some slant light,
the beloved arriving—
again, again—
each one carrying
a small illegal joy
wrapped in the plain brown paper
of an ordinary face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in the style of a modern American poet (like Frank O'Hara) about watching someone return home, mixing tenderness and unease?
counterfactuals.output:
**Coming Up the Walk**

I see you from the window before you see me seeing you,
keys already out, shoulders doing that thing they do
when the day has been too much or not enough—
I can never tell which tires you more.

There's a dog barking three yards down like it's rehearsed,
and the streetlight hasn't decided yet if it's dusk or committed,
and you're walking like someone who has walked this exact
distance four thousand times and still doesn't trust the sidewalk.

I want to say I've been fine. I want to say the coffee's hot
and I didn't just check the clock nine times in the last hour,
didn't just replay the version where you don't come up the walk at all,
where the door stays a door and not a threshold you cross back into me.

You're closer now. I can see you're chewing the inside of your cheek,
a habit I love and worry over in the same breath,
the way I love and worry over weather,
the way the news becomes personal if you squint at it long enough.

Here's the thing about doors: they open both ways
and I never know which way you're opening it from—
toward me, like a question,
or through me, like weather passing, necessary, unstoppable.

I put the coffee down. I arrange my face
into something like ease, something like *I wasn't worried*,
though the whole apartment still smells like the version of me
that spent the afternoon inventing reasons you'd be late.

The key turns. That particular music.
I am so glad. I am already exhausted
by how glad I am, how much room this gladness takes,
how it sits down at the table like it's staying for dinner,

like it isn't going anywhere,
like tomorrow this doesn't happen all over again—
the watching, the waiting, the door as a wound
that keeps closing and calling it healing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that personifies arrival and longing, with metaphors comparing a person's movements to animals (crabs, turtles, tugboats) and ending on a reflective note about love's origins.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Remembers

She comes sideways into rooms,
crab-quick, all elbow and hinge,
scuttling toward the light
then away from it,
as if love were a shell
she could duck into
whenever the tide turned wrong.

He arrives like something ancient,
turtle-slow, dragging
the whole weight of his shelter
across linoleum and years,
patient in the way stones are patient,
believing the distance
will forgive him if he's honest
about how long it takes.

And longing—longing is a tugboat,
small and stubborn in the harbor,
pushing against hulls
ten times its size,
insisting that the enormous thing
can still be moved,
can still be brought to shore
if you just keep leaning
your whole small body
into the work of wanting.

We meet like weather systems,
never quite arriving,
always in the process of becoming close—
her sideways glance,
his slow unfolding,
the tug and pull of something
neither of us named yet.

I think love starts this way:
not with a door flung open
but with creatures finding
their own strange methods
of approach—
the crab's oblique devotion,
the turtle's ancient patience,
the tugboat's small, insistent faith
that even distance
can be worked into arrival,

that even the heaviest things
can be nudged, eventually,
toward each other,

if something small enough
keeps believing
it was built for exactly this—

the moving of what matters
across whatever water
keeps us apart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
